transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I'm just so exhausted, doctor... I've been struggling with really severe depression and having absolutely no energy for over two years now. On top of that, I've been hearing voices and feeling constantly paranoid, and it's just gotten too difficult to manage on my own.
Have the voices or paranoia ever happened for at least two weeks when you were not feeling depressed or having mood symptoms?

Yes, that has definitely happened. There were times, lasting at least two or three weeks, where my mood actually felt relatively okay, but the voices and the feeling of being watched were still completely there. It made me realize that the paranoia doesn't just go away when the depression lifts.
Have you ever had a period of at least a few days where you felt unusually energized or irritable, needed much less sleep, talked more than usual, or did risky things?
No, I've never experienced anything like that. I actually feel the exact opposite—usually very tired, drained, and down. I've never had periods of high energy or needing less sleep.
Do your depression symptoms happen only during the times when you have voices or paranoia, or have there also been long periods of depression without any psychotic symptoms?

Yes, there have definitely been long periods where I felt deeply depressed but didn't have any of the voices or paranoia. The heavy sadness and lack of energy seem to stay with me almost constantly, even during the times when those other things quiet down.
Have you ever had a period of at least one month where the voices or paranoia were present but your depression was not?

Yes, there was a period of about a month where my mood actually improved and I didn't feel depressed at all. However, during that entire time, I was still hearing the voices and felt constantly paranoid. It was really confusing because I felt better emotionally, but those scary experiences didn't stop.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [Schizophrenia, Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)], but the interview shows psychotic symptoms persisting for at least 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms, and also at least 1 month of psychosis without depression. That pattern rules out schizoaffective disorder, because mood episodes are not present for the majority of the illness. The remaining best fit is Schizophrenia.

inference_history.note: Previously there were no candidates provided. Based on this initial report, the key features are a >2-year depressive syndrome with psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and paranoia). Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is a leading possibility if psychotic symptoms have occurred for at least 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features remains possible if psychosis occurs only during depressive episodes. Schizophrenia is also on the differential because of persistent hallucinations and paranoia, though the prominent chronic depression makes a primary mood disorder with psychosis more likely.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a prolonged major depressive syndrome for over two years plus persistent psychotic symptoms (voices, paranoia) that clearly occur for at least 2 weeks and even about 1 month in the absence of mood symptoms. This rules out major depressive disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis occurs only during depression. The chronic psychosis with substantial mood symptoms is most consistent with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
